title: Capturing luck: use "or" paths instead of stacking "and" requirements
summary: Startups need many things to go right at once, and multiplying those probabilities makes success unlikely. Jason Cohen argues you can improve your odds by reducing the number of "and" dependencies and building in many parallel "or" paths, because optionality is strength.

principles.text: Startup success is a chain of "and" requirements, so total odds are the product of each probability.
principles.quote: Each one has a probability of success, and you compute the total probability of success by multiplying them.

principles.text: Even optimistic odds collapse when many things must all go right.
principles.quote: 70% multiplied by itself six times is only 12%; most of these things we're listing have a probability less than 70%, and there are more than six things that have to go right.

principles.text: Remove "and" risks up front by choosing a big, healthy market and a niche where incumbents don't care.
principles.quote: You can pick a large, growing, and healthy market so that the risk that "no one wants to solve this problem" goes to zero.

principles.text: Reduce people risk by hiring someone you've worked with before, or avoiding the hire entirely.
principles.quote: You can hire someone you've worked with before, or build something sustainable without hiring.

principles.text: Stack "or" options: you only need one acquisition channel to work, so try several.
principles.quote: Only one of these needs to work! So although the probability of success for each one of these is low, the probability that *something* will work is higher.

principles.text: Optionality is strength: many ways to win is a strong position even before any of them has worked.
principles.quote: The general rule is **optionality is strength.** When there are lots of ways for things to go right, that is a strong position even if you haven't actualized one of those ways.
